title: Direct Use of a Tweakable Blockcipher as a TCC
summary: A TBC has TCC syntax, but an inverse-based attack shows it is not collision resistant; the unresolved task concerns whether it can be used directly in the TCC role.

formal_statement.body: Determine whether a tweakable blockcipher (TBC), which has the syntax of the target TCC primitive, can be used directly in the TCC role while satisfying collision resistance. The central limitation is a collision attack on a TBC $F$: choose arbitrary $CK$ and $D_1$, choose distinct tweaks $T_1$ and $T_2$, and set $D_2 \leftarrow F.\operatorname{Inv}(CK,T_2,F.\operatorname{Ev}(CK,T_1,D_1))$; then $(CK,T_1,D_1)$ and $(CK,T_2,D_2)$ form a collision, so $F$ is not collision resistant.

scope.domain: Tweakable blockciphers and TCCs, focusing on collision resistance.
parameters: TBC F as the candidate TCC primitive
CK and D1 as arbitrary inputs in the attack
T1 and T2 as distinct tweaks
scope.unresolved_remainder: Determine whether a tweakable blockcipher can be used directly in the TCC role while satisfying collision resistance.

citations.label: A Universal Transform for Committing Authenticated Encryption

progress.summary: The source explicitly asks why a syntactically compatible TBC cannot simply be used as a TCC. It presents an inverse-based collision attack showing that a TBC is not collision resistant.
